This minute body mass, typical of anurans that undergo an extended larval phase, marks the beginning of a rapid growth trajectory. At the point of metamorphosis, when the tail is fully resorbed and the juvenile body plan is established, individuals attain a snout-vent length of approximately 1.7 centimeters . This length is measured as the distance from the tip of the snout to the vent, a standard metric in amphibian morphometrics. The transition from aquatic tadpole to terrestrial juvenile represents a critical period of high mortality, and the size at which metamorphosis occurs can influence subsequent survival and growth rates. The relatively small size at emergence from the egg contrasts sharply with the dimensions achieved by reproductively mature adults, underscoring the substantial somatic investment required during the larval and juvenile stages.

At this developmental milestone, the gonads become fully functional and males begin to participate in breeding choruses. Females, in contrast, follow a delayed maturation schedule, with puberty occurring at a larger body size of about 5.5 centimeters [Lp = about 5.5 centimeters]. This sexual dimorphism in size at maturity is a common pattern among ranid frogs, often attributed to fecundity selection, as larger females can accommodate more eggs. Males, by comparison, reach pubertal mass at approximately 10.8 grams [Wwp = approximately 10.8 grams], a lower figure consistent with their reduced investment in gamete production.
